clues.text: At atomic levels, this force is explained by the Tomlinson model, used by nano-tribologists.
Surfaces known as asperities help to explain the presence of this force at microscopic levels.
This phenomenon is governed by Amontons’ laws and has a “dry” variety modeled by an equation named for Coulomb.
Magnetic levitation avoids the “rolling” type of this force typically experienced by cars.
According to Amonton’s laws, this force is independent of the total area of contact between objects and, unless the objects are not moving, is independent of the velocity of motion.
Drag is sometimes known as the air type of this phenomenon, and Coulomb names its simplified dry type.
This force’s coefficient, mu, can be reduced by applying a lubricant.
For a given object, the kinetic variety is less than the static type.
Name this force that resists motion, as seen when trying to slide a box on sandpaper.
Name this force that resists the motion of an object.

answerlines: diffraction [or far-field diffraction; or near-field diffraction; prompt on interference; do NOT accept “refraction” or “rarefaction”]

clues.text: A common demonstration of this phenomenon uses it to measure the width of a strand of hair.
A pattern produced by this phenomenon is proportional to the square of the sinc function.
Fraunhofer and Fresnel (“fruh-NELL”) name the far-field and near-field types of this phenomenon, respectively.
The opacity of an object will only affect the intensity of this process according to Babinet's principle, which holds that it behaves identically for an object and an equivalent hole.
A law governing this phenomenon states that “n times lambda equals 2d sine theta."
Rosalind Franklin employed this phenomenon with X-rays to obtain images of DNA.
Crystals can create this phenomenon in X-rays, as described by Bragg's law, and crystal structure can be determined from the resulting pattern.
Interference caused by this phenomenon creates alternating light and dark bands, which was observed in Young’s double-slit experiment.
Name this phenomenon that explains the interference fringes in Young’s double slit experiment, the process by which light bends when passing through an aperture.
Name this term for the bending of light around an obstacle.

answerlines: titration [or titrimetry or volumetric analysis; accept titrating or Fischer titration or acid-base titration or redox titration or volumetric titration or coulometric titration]

clues.text: A “checkerboard” form of this procedure is used before ELISA.
One form of this technique uses an alcohol and base solution to facilitate the oxidation of sulfur dioxide with iodine to determine trace water in a sample.
This method is sometimes performed in a non-aqueous solution to avoid the leveling effect.

An anode containing a base, an alcohol, iodine, and sulfur dioxide is employed in a form of this procedure developed by Karl Fischer, and the distinctive colors displayed when EDTA chelates metal ions contrast with those of organic dyes in the complexometric form.
Sodium thiosulfate is used as a reducing agent in a version of this technique that uses a solution of iodine and starch.
Plots corresponding to this procedure display at least one inflection point.
Plotting a graph of the progress of this technique versus potential or pH creates a curve with a notable inflection point.
Completion of this technique is determined through the color change of an indicator like phenolphthalein at the endpoint.
Phenolphthalein (“fee-nol-thay-leen”) is commonly used as an indicator in the acid-base form of this technique.
Name this analytical chemistry technique that measures the concentration of an unknown solution.
